Trying to Conceive

Low sperm vitality: confirming necrozoospermia and planning care

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Seeing “dead sperm” or “low vitality” on a report can be alarming. The first task is to establish what was measured and whether the finding is reliable. Some samples contain living sperm that do not move, and some contain a mixture of living and dead cells. A careful distinction helps the team plan an appropriate investigation and realistic fertility options.

A sperm can be still and alive

Sperm motility describes movement; vitality describes whether sperm are alive. Asthenozoospermia means reduced motility. Some sperm that do not move still have an intact, functioning membrane and may be usable in fertility treatment. Looking only at movement cannot establish that every immotile sperm is dead.

Necrozoospermia means an abnormally low proportion of living sperm in a semen sample. It does not necessarily mean that all sperm are dead. Complete or absolute necrozoospermia describes a sample in which no living sperm are identified after appropriate testing. That is different from azoospermia, where no sperm are found. These distinctions change what needs confirming and which options may be considered.

A reference value is not a verdict on fertility

Current EAU guidance lists 54% living sperm as the 2021 lower reference value for vitality. This describes the lower end of a reference population, not a boundary that separates everyone who can conceive from everyone who cannot. It is also a percentage of living sperm, not a percentage of dead sperm. Different historical thresholds and study-specific severity groups should not be mixed together.

Ask which test and reference range your report uses, and whether any living sperm were found. The whole semen pattern and both partners’ reproductive circumstances matter. A low vitality result alone cannot supply a personal pregnancy rate, identify its cause or show that treatment is impossible. Avoid comparing a single number with an online “mild” or “severe” chart without that context.

Confirm what the laboratory actually measured

A vitality assessment is particularly useful when many sperm are immotile. WHO-based practice commonly uses a diagnostic stain such as eosin–nigrosin: cells with damaged membranes take up the dye, while cells with intact membranes exclude it. Other methods, including the hypo-osmotic swelling test, assess membrane function differently. A report should make clear which method was used.

An embryology laboratory may need a different, non-destructive method when selecting a living, immotile sperm for treatment. Sperm exposed to a diagnostic stain are not simply taken from that stained preparation and injected into an egg. Ask whether the result came from a diagnostic assessment or a treatment-selection procedure. These tests belong in a qualified laboratory and cannot be reproduced reliably with a home microscope.

Review collection and transport before drawing conclusions

Some samples are affected by unapproved lubricant, saliva, soap residue, water, an unsuitable container or a consumer condom. A condom labelled non-spermicidal is not automatically approved for semen testing. Delays, dehydration or unsuitable temperatures can also affect interpretation. Tell the laboratory what actually happened; do not hide a problem or assume that a product advertised as fertility-friendly was suitable for this test.

For another sample, use the receiving laboratory’s approved supplies and written instructions. Report the collection time, abstinence interval, missed portions and any delay. A clinician may request confirmation under better-controlled conditions or at a specialist laboratory. These precautions do not mean that most low-vitality diagnoses are mistakes. A confirmed abnormal result deserves assessment rather than repeated dismissal as a collection error.

Look for a cause without assuming one from the result

The specialist may review recent fever, infection symptoms, medicines and nonmedical drugs, repeated heat exposure, previous surgery, testicular or epididymal problems, and relevant hormone or neurological conditions. Examination and selected tests help decide which possibilities are credible. A list of possible contributors is not proof that a particular habit, medicine, age or disability caused your result.

Some problems arise during sperm production; others may develop as sperm pass through or are stored in the reproductive tract. A 2025 retrospective study of more than 300 patients found an association between seminal-tract abnormalities and more severe low vitality. That finding does not diagnose an obstruction in every patient or establish a treatment that works for everyone. Sometimes no clear cause is found despite an appropriate evaluation.

Treat identified problems rather than the label alone

A confirmed infection may need treatment, but low vitality by itself does not establish a bacterial infection or justify antibiotics. Likewise, hormone treatment is appropriate only for selected diagnoses. Testosterone taken from outside the body can suppress sperm production and is not a general infertility treatment. Discuss prescribed medicines with the responsible clinician instead of stopping or changing them yourself.

Ask what each proposed treatment is intended to improve and how that improvement will be assessed. A change in a laboratory percentage is not the same as a demonstrated increase in live birth. Supplements and antioxidants should not be presented as a proven cure for every low-vitality result. If a varicocele or another condition is found, its treatment decision should account for the complete assessment and the time available for both partners.

A second sample or different interval may have a specific purpose

Repeat testing can answer different questions: whether the first sample was affected by collection, whether the finding persists, or whether another ejaculate contains usable living sperm for treatment. Those purposes do not always require the same interval. Ask why your timing was chosen, and do not postpone specialist advice about a severe result merely to follow a general waiting period found online.

Very small older studies, including a three-couple report from 1998 and a four-case report from 1988, explored frequent ejaculation in selected patients. They cannot establish a reliable live-birth benefit or a universal schedule. ESHRE’s 2026 laboratory recommendations also distinguish diagnostic standardization from treatment collection and note the limited evidence for consecutive ejaculates as routine practice. Follow a planned laboratory request rather than designing a repeated-ejaculation regimen yourself.

Living sperm in the ejaculate may still offer options

If some sperm are alive, the fertility team can assess whether enough suitable cells can be identified for the proposed treatment. Complete immotility does not automatically require surgery when living sperm can be selected. Conversely, ICSI cannot be assumed to solve the problem simply by injecting a sperm that has been confirmed dead.

ICSI is performed within IVF: an embryologist injects a selected sperm into an egg. It can help overcome particular sperm-related fertilization difficulties, but fertilization is only one step. Egg-related factors, embryo development and other circumstances still affect the chance of a baby. The procedure can damage some eggs. Ask how the clinic will identify usable sperm and what the backup plan is if none are found on the treatment day.

Surgical retrieval is a specialist option with limits

When repeated, properly assessed ejaculates contain no usable living sperm, testicular retrieval may be considered. TESE takes a small tissue sample through an incision; TESA uses a needle to aspirate from the testicle. Procedures involving the epididymis have different names and indications. These terms should not be used interchangeably, and a low-vitality result does not by itself decide which procedure is appropriate.

A 2014 retrospective study of incomplete necrozoospermia reported better live-birth outcomes with testicular than ejaculated sperm in its selected patients. It did not randomly assign treatment and cannot prove surgery is best for every patient. Retrieval may fail to find usable sperm, and successful retrieval does not guarantee a baby. Bleeding, infection and a possible fall in testosterone are relevant risks to discuss before consent.

Retrieving sperm is not the same as maturing any germ cell

The aim of a retrieval plan is to find sperm that the laboratory can assess and use appropriately. It should not be described as a guaranteed process in which immature cells are removed, grown into normal sperm and injected routinely. Cells at different developmental stages are biologically different, even when they all come from testicular tissue.

Methods involving immature round spermatids are distinct from conventional ICSI using spermatozoa. ASRM’s 2008 committee opinion described unresolved safety and technical issues with this experimental approach; that older document is not a statement of every country’s current rules. If a clinic proposes an unusual technique, ask exactly which cell is being used, whether the method is established care or research, and what evidence supports the expected benefit.

Difficulty ejaculating needs its own collection plan

A spinal cord injury or another neurological condition can affect ejaculation as well as semen findings. Difficulty obtaining a sample is not proof that all sperm are dead. Explain accessibility needs and previous collection difficulties before treatment so the team can arrange a suitable method and a contingency plan.

For selected people with anejaculation, specialist options include penile vibratory stimulation and, when appropriate, electro-ejaculation or sperm retrieval. EAU guidance places these within a clinical pathway; electro-ejaculation is not a home treatment with electrical shocks. The choice depends on the underlying condition and safety assessment. It should not be prescribed simply because someone uses a wheelchair or has a low vitality percentage.

Agree on next steps and keep urgent symptoms separate

Ask for a written plan covering confirmation, likely causes, treatment options, uncertainty and what happens if no usable sperm can be obtained. Counselling can support decisions about further treatment, donor sperm or other personal paths; there is no single correct choice for every family. A fertility result is not a measure of masculinity or personal worth.

Sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency care. So does testicular pain accompanied by nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain. Pain lasting more than an hour or persisting at rest also needs emergency care. Arrange a driver or an ambulance instead of driving yourself. New lumps, swelling, changes in testicle shape or feel, or worrying discomfort need urgent medical advice. Do not wait for repeat semen testing or a fertility appointment to address those symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

WHO laboratory methods and EAU guidance distinguish vitality from movement and emphasize interpretable samples. A lower reference value should not be used as an individual fertility verdict.

Evidence specific to repeated ejaculation and testicular versus ejaculated sperm in necrozoospermia is limited. Small case reports and retrospective comparisons cannot establish a universal schedule or the best treatment for everyone.

Current laboratory recommendations support careful selection of living sperm when motility is absent. Diagnostic staining, treatment selection, surgical retrieval and experimental immature-cell techniques are different procedures.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare questions about confirmation, the purpose of further tests and realistic options. A reproductive specialist and qualified laboratory need to interpret the findings and agree a plan with you.

When to seek help

Do not change prescribed medicines or attempt laboratory or electrical collection procedures yourself. Sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or at rest needs emergency care; arrange transport rather than driving yourself. New lumps, swelling or concerning changes need urgent advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Movement and vitality are different: an immotile sperm can still be alive.
  • Confirm the method, collection conditions and repeat plan before treating a single result as final.
  • Investigate likely causes and avoid unsupported antibiotic, hormone or supplement treatment.
  • ICSI needs suitable sperm; neither laboratory selection nor surgical retrieval guarantees a baby.
  • Ask for a backup plan and seek urgent care for testicular symptoms independently of fertility testing.

Frequently asked questions

What causes necrozoospermia?

Possible causes involve sperm production, the reproductive tract, infection, heat exposure, medicines or other medical conditions. A result alone cannot identify the cause, and sometimes it remains unclear after assessment.

Which risk factors should I mention to the specialist?

Report recent fever, infection symptoms, medicines and supplements, nonmedical drugs, significant heat or chemical exposure, previous surgery, neurological conditions and collection problems. These details guide evaluation; they do not prove that any one factor caused the finding.

How is asthenozoospermia different?

Asthenozoospermia describes reduced sperm movement. Necrozoospermia describes reduced vitality, meaning fewer living sperm. A laboratory test may show that an immotile sperm is still alive, which can change treatment choices.

How is necrozoospermia treated?

First confirm the result and investigate plausible causes. Treatment may address an identified condition or involve specialist sperm selection, IVF with ICSI or selected retrieval procedures. There is no universal medicine or operation that guarantees success.

Does 54% vitality determine whether I can have a child?

No. The 54% lower reference value is not a fertile–infertile boundary. The method, complete semen pattern, repeat findings and both partners’ circumstances need interpretation.

Can an ejaculated sample be used for ICSI?

Sometimes, if suitable living sperm can be identified. Low vitality does not necessarily mean that every sperm is dead. The laboratory must assess the actual sample and explain its selection and backup plan.

Should I ejaculate repeatedly before the next test?

Only follow the interval requested for that specific assessment or treatment. Small studies do not justify a universal regimen, and diagnostic collection instructions may differ from a specialist request for another treatment sample.

Does testicular sperm retrieval guarantee a baby?

No. Usable sperm may not be found, and finding them does not guarantee fertilization, pregnancy or live birth. Ask about the procedure, alternatives, risks and expected outcomes in patients with similar findings.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
